title.en: Impersonal constructions: его́ ра́нило, мне не спи́тся

card: Beyond **мне хо́лодно**, Russian uses impersonal verbs where English needs a subject. Natural forces: **Доро́гу занесло́ сне́гом** (the road was snowed over). Involuntary states: **Мне не спи́тся** (I can't get to sleep). Lack: **Мне не хвата́ет вре́мени**. Success and luck: **Нам удало́сь**, **Мне повезло́**.

sections.body: These sentences present events as happening *to* people, by forces no one controls. They're everywhere in literature and common in speech; English can only paraphrase them.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
rows: neuter past, the affected thing in the accusative, the force in the instrumental
**не** + verb + **-ся**, the person in the dative

sections.title: Tense and agreement
sections.body: Impersonal verbs stay in the third person singular, neuter in the past: **Мне не хвата́ло де́нег.** **Нам повезло́.** What's lacking is genitive, not a subject: not ~~Мне не хвата́ют де́ньги~~.

sections.title: Personal or impersonal?
sections.body: **Я не сплю** is a fact (*I'm not asleep*); **Мне не спи́тся** says sleep won't come, against my will. **Ве́тер унёс ло́дку** names the wind as a doer; **Ло́дку унесло́ ве́тром** describes something that just happened.

mistakes.why: **хвата́ть** is impersonal: a singular verb, and the genitive of what's lacking.
**удава́ться** takes the dative of the person.

examples.en: I can't get to sleep tonight.
He was wounded in the war.
